Jessica selects one of the $2^3-1=7$ non-empty subsets uniformly at random, so each has prior probability $\frac17$.

Let $E$ be the observed draws (red, blue, red). A subset can only produce this outcome if it contains at least one red and at least one blue marble. Thus only two subsets have non-zero likelihood:

- **Subset $\{R,B\}$:** The bag has 1 red and 1 blue. Drawing with replacement gives $P(R)=P(B)=\frac12$, so
  $$P(E \mid \{R,B\}) = \left(\frac12\right)\left(\frac12\right)\left(\frac12\right) = \frac18.$$

- **Subset $\{R,G,B\}$:** The bag has one of each color, so $P(R)=P(B)=\frac13$, giving
  $$P(E \mid \{R,G,B\}) = \left(\frac13\right)\left(\frac13\right)\left(\frac13\right) = \frac1{27}.$$

All other subsets have likelihood $0$.

By Bayes' theorem, the posterior probability that the bag contains only red and blue is proportional to its prior times its likelihood:
$$P(\{R,B\} \mid E) = \frac{\frac17 \cdot \frac18}{\frac17 \cdot \frac18 + \frac17 \cdot \frac1{27}} = \frac{\frac18}{\frac18 + \frac1{27}}.$$

Simplifying:
$$\frac{\frac18}{\frac{27+8}{216}} = \frac{27}{35}.$$

(If one interprets the observation as "two reds and one blue in any order" rather than that exact sequence, the combinatorial factor $\binom{3}{2}=3$ appears in both the numerator and denominator and cancels, yielding the same result.)

$$\boxed{\frac{27}{35}}$$
